ChZDSUhNMG9nS0VJQ0FnSUMwcUlYUEhBEAE:
Visited on September 13, 2019.
Among the many dentists in Bangkok, this is a well-known dentist with an established reputation among Japanese people.
As a frequent visitor to many veterans who have lived in Bangkok for over 20 years, this dentist is a must-visit when it comes to reasonable treatment fees, quality of treatment, and the peace of mind of knowing they can communicate in Japanese.
There may be better dentists in Bangkok, but this is my personal choice.
Fluent Japanese is a challenge, but communication is sufficient with simple Japanese.
If you encounter a dentist who doesn't speak Japanese, a Japanese-speaking staff member will act as an interpreter.
However, since this is not an ultra-high-end dentist, you may be somewhat overwhelmed... But the peace of mind of having an interpreter, even if just for a brief moment, is great.
I had a filling reattached to a missing tooth for 900 baht (3,200 yen), a full self-pay fee not covered by insurance.
I also had tartar removed for the same 900 baht.
I'm happy that simple treatments can be completed in a day.
ChZDSUhNMG9nS0VJQ0FnSURDbktpVEJREAE:
This dentist on Sukhumvit 49 is popular with many Japanese people. There are several dentists catering to Japanese people in Bangkok's Phrom Phong and Thonglor areas, but this is one of the more popular.

When you call, you'll be surprised to hear, "Hello, this is the dentist..." but you can make an appointment in Japanese. It's not that the staff are rude, they just don't speak Japanese that well. They were fully booked for about a week, so I made an appointment for the earliest available date and time.

The staff can also speak Japanese, so it's reassuring. I was worried the fees would be extremely high, but I was pleased that they weren't that expensive: 100 baht for the consultation, 1,500 baht for simple cavity treatment, and 1,500 baht for tartar removal.
Ci9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT2tod1ZEQkVPRFZ2:
It's near Sammy Debate Hospital. There's a sign, so it was easy to find.

ChdDSUhNMG9nS0VJQ0FnSUNSaGRqcC13RRAB:
I had a ceramic crown on one of my back teeth repaired because it had cracked. The Japanese-language support during the booking process was excellent, which was reassuring. Dr. Pongsak treated me; his Japanese was excellent, and his treatment plan was very clear and understandable. It felt almost like being treated by a Japanese dentist. The treatment only took about 30 minutes and was completed in one day, which I appreciated. The cost was 2,100 baht, which I don't think is expensive. The only drawback is that it's a bit far from the BTS station; it's closer from Thonglor. It's nice that you can shop at Fuji Supermarket on the way back, though.

As an aside, I was surprised that the receptionist was fluent in Chinese (he was dealing with Chinese customers). He also seemed to speak English, so it looks like they can handle four languages.

I went to this dental clinic because my dental crown fell out. I don't have any other comparable experiences in Bangkok, but personally, I'd give it a passing grade.

They took an X-ray of a portion of my tooth and fixed the missing crown in place, and the total cost was 1200 baht. In Japan, there's usually a consultation fee plus you pay 30% of that, so I think this is slightly cheaper. They also fill out the paperwork for insurance claims when you return home.

The dentist's Japanese is broken, but the receptionist translated for me. The receptionist also spoke Chinese, so I think they see many foreigners as well as Japanese patients.
ChdDSUhNMG9nS0VJQ0FnSUN3emFxWl93RRAB: I felt reassured knowing that the dentist spoke Japanese, but I regret not having communicated more thoroughly with them, as I am Thai and not fluent in Japanese. I don't know about other dentists, but even though Japanese health insurance can be used after applying for it after returning to Japan, the original treatment costs are higher than in Japan, so be careful.
ChdDSUhNMG9nS0VJQ0FnSUN3azZ2cDRRRRAB:
Japanese is OK

I use this dental clinic. Japanese is OK. It's by appointment only, but if you're in pain and just walk in, they'll let you in. When you call, they'll initially speak Thai, but once they realize you're speaking Japanese or Thai spoken by a Japanese person, they'll switch to Japanese. The doctors speak Japanese, and there's a nurse who acts as an interpreter.

In Thailand, dental treatment is usually completed in one visit, but even in general, dental care, including cavity treatment, anesthesia, and extractions, is performed by specialists. If the specialist isn't available for treatment, even if you walk in, you'll only receive emergency treatment and will need to come back another time.

It's more expensive than a local dentist, but cheaper than a large private hospital. Insurance is accepted.
